summary: Croatia has been a full Schengen Area member since January 2023: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, around 60 visa-exempt nationalities can stay 90 days in any 180-day period (with the ETIAS travel authorisation being phased in), and everyone else needs a Schengen short-stay visa costing €90.

visaTypes.name: Long-Stay Visa (Type D) / Temporary Stay Permit

fee.notes: For stays over 90 days: work, study, family and other long-stay purposes, usually processed together with a temporary stay permit. Fees vary by category.
For courses longer than 90 days; needs proof of enrolment at a Croatian institution, funds, accommodation and health insurance. Fees vary by category.
Combined residence and work permit for employment over 90 days; the employer in Croatia usually initiates the application. Fees vary by category.

passportValidity.text: Non-EU passports must be valid for at least 3 months beyond your planned departure from the Schengen Area and have been issued within the last 10 years.

travelInsurance.text: Schengen visa applicants must hold travel medical insurance covering at least €30,000, valid across the Schengen Area for the whole stay. Visa-exempt visitors are not required to show it but border officers may ask about cover.

onwardTicket.text: Border officers may ask non-EU visitors for proof of return or onward travel and accommodation details.

proofOfFunds.text: Croatia's reference amount for non-EU visitors is around €70 per person per day, reduced to about €30 per day if accommodation is paid in advance or you have an invitation letter.

declarations.name: EES — Entry/Exit System (biometric registration)
declarations.submitWindow: At the border on first entry
declarations.text: Non-EU travellers are registered biometrically (fingerprints and photo) in the EU Entry/Exit System at Schengen external borders. Registration happens at the border — there is nothing to submit in advance, but allow extra time on your first entry.

declarations.name: ETIAS — European Travel Information and Authorisation System

fee.notes: Free for under-18s and over-70s. Valid 3 years or until passport expiry.

declarations.text: Visa-exempt travellers will need an ETIAS travel authorisation to enter the Schengen Area. It is being phased in — check the official EU site for the current status and apply only there.

currencyLimits.text: Cash of €10,000 or more (or equivalent) must be declared when entering or leaving the EU.

notes: Duty-free from outside the EU: 200 cigarettes, 1 litre of spirits, goods up to €300 (€430 arriving by air/sea).
No limits on goods for personal use when arriving from another EU country.
Full border checks apply when crossing to and from Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia and Montenegro — these are external Schengen borders.

payments.text: Croatia adopted the euro in January 2023. Cards and contactless payments are accepted almost everywhere; keep some cash for small konobas, markets and island kiosks.

safety.text: Croatia is one of Europe's safest destinations, with low crime even in peak tourist season. Petty theft can occur in crowded old towns and on beaches.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Croatia Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: May–June and September are ideal for the Adriatic coast — warm sea, lower prices and far fewer crowds than the July–August peak; spring and autumn also suit Zagreb and the national parks.

tips.text: The 90-day limit counts across the entire Schengen Area, not just Croatia — days spent in Italy or Slovenia count against the same allowance.
Croatia charges a small tourist tax per person per night (roughly €1–2, higher in peak season), usually collected by your accommodation and sometimes payable in cash.
Book island car ferries and catamarans (Jadrolinija, Krilo) well in advance in July–August — vehicle spaces sell out and foot passengers face long queues in Split and Dubrovnik.
First-time EES biometric registration can add queue time — allow margin at airports and at land crossings from Bosnia, Serbia and Montenegro, which are external Schengen borders.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Croatia?
faq.answer: No. US passport holders can visit Croatia and the rest of the Schengen Area visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. Once ETIAS becomes mandatory, they will need to obtain this online authorisation (€20) before travel.

faq.question: Is Croatia in the Schengen Area and does it use the euro?
faq.answer: Yes to both. Croatia joined the Schengen Area and adopted the euro on 1 January 2023, so there are no border checks when arriving from other Schengen countries and prices are in euros.

faq.question: How much does a Croatia Schengen visa cost?
faq.answer: The Schengen short-stay visa costs €90 for adults and €45 for children aged 6–11. It allows stays of up to 90 days in any 180-day period across all Schengen countries, and applications are decided within 15–45 calendar days.

faq.question: Is ETIAS required to enter Croatia?
faq.answer: ETIAS is being phased in for visa-exempt travellers. During the transition period travellers without ETIAS are still admitted; once fully mandatory, the €20 online authorisation will be required before boarding. Check the official EU website for the current status.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Croatia without a visa?
faq.answer: Visa-exempt non-EU visitors can stay up to 90 days within any 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area. EU and EFTA citizens can stay indefinitely but must register locally after 3 months.
